subject: Archaeology
title: Potassium-Argon Dating: Deep Time
description: A fast breakdown of Potassium-Argon Dating: Deep Time for builders.

hook.text: Radiocarbon dating stops working after 50,000 years. For older sites, scientists use volcanoes as their clock.

buildup.text: Potassium in volcanic rock decays into argon gas. The gas gets trapped in cooled lava, and its amount reveals the age.

discovery.text: This method dated the oldest human ancestors. The volcanic ash above and below Lucy placed her at 3.2 million years old.

twist.text: It only works on volcanic layers, not the fossils themselves. You date the rock sandwich around the find.

climax.text: Potassium-argon dating proved humans evolved in Africa millions of years ago — the evidence that settled the origin.

punchline.text: Volcanoes set the clock. Fossils just happened to be in between the eruptions.

quiz.question: How does potassium-argon dating work?
options: It measures potassium levels in fossilized bone tissue
It measures argon gas trapped in volcanic rock that formed around fossils
It tracks potassium decay in ancient pottery and metal tools

details.summary: Potassium-argon dating measures the decay of potassium-40 to argon-40 in volcanic rocks, dating materials from 100,000 to billions of years old. It is essential for dating early human sites in East Africa, where volcanic ash layers bracket hominin fossils and stone tools.
details.whyItMatters: Without potassium-argon dating, the timeline of human evolution would be unknown. It dates the volcanic layers surrounding the oldest human ancestors in East Africa, providing the chronological framework for our origin story.
takeaways: Dates volcanic rocks from 100,000 to billions of years old
Essential for dating early human sites in East Africa
Measures decay of potassium-40 to argon-40 in minerals

faq.question: Why is potassium-argon dating so important for human evolution?
faq.answer: Early human fossils in East Africa's Rift Valley are found between volcanic ash layers. Dating these volcanic deposits with potassium-argon provides maximum and minimum ages for the fossils. Without this method, the ages of Lucy, Homo erectus, and other key specimens would be unknown.

faq.question: Can potassium-argon dating be used on recent sites?
faq.answer: Its minimum range is about 100,000 years, too old for most archaeological sites. The related argon-argon method improves precision for younger volcanic deposits. For sites under 50,000 years, radiocarbon and other methods are more appropriate.
